title: What Is Randomness? Can Anything Truly Be Random?
question: Is there such a thing as genuine randomness in the universe, or is everything we call 'random' just complexity we haven't traced back to its causes yet?
summary: From dice to quantum decay to the pseudo-random numbers inside your phone, 'random' turns out to be a surprisingly slippery word, and physics itself splits into two camps about whether true randomness exists at all.
content:
Flip a coin, and most people call the outcome random. But a coin flip is entirely governed by classical physics — its spin, height, and landing are determined by the force of the flick, air resistance, and gravity. In principle, a being with perfect knowledge of the initial conditions could predict the result every time. Is that randomness, or just ignorance dressed up as chance? The question turns out to reach into some of the deepest disagreements in physics, mathematics, and computer science.

Two Very Different Kinds of "Random"

It helps to separate epistemic randomness from ontological randomness. Epistemic randomness is randomness of ignorance: a system is fully deterministic, but we lack the information or computational power to predict it, so it looks random to us. Coin flips, dice rolls, shuffled cards, and weather all fall into this category — chaotic, sensitive to tiny variations, but governed by fixed physical laws underneath. Ontological randomness, by contrast, would mean the outcome is genuinely undetermined even in principle, with no hidden variable anywhere that fixes it in advance. The only serious candidate for this in physics is quantum mechanics.

The Quantum Claim

According to the standard interpretation of quantum mechanics, the decay time of a specific radioactive atom, or the outcome of measuring a particle's spin, is not merely unknown but fundamentally undetermined until measured. This isn't a claim about our ignorance; it's built into the mathematical structure of the theory itself. Bell's theorem, tested experimentally many times since the 1970s, rules out a wide class of "hidden variable" explanations that would let quantum outcomes secretly be predetermined. If quantum mechanics is right, and if those experiments are interpreted correctly, the universe contains events with no cause that fixes their outcome — true, irreducible randomness.

But Not Everyone Agrees

Not every serious physicist accepts this. Deterministic interpretations of quantum mechanics exist, most famously Bohmian mechanics, which restores a fully deterministic underlying reality by adding hidden variables that are non-local rather than local — reproducing every experimental prediction of standard quantum theory while denying that anything is ever truly random. The "many-worlds" interpretation takes a different tack: it denies that any randomness occurs at all, proposing instead that every possible outcome happens, in different branching universes, and the appearance of randomness is just an artifact of which branch you happen to find yourself in. So even at the frontier of physics, whether true randomness exists depends partly on an interpretive choice we don't yet have a definitive experiment to settle.

Randomness You Can Build and Sell

Meanwhile, engineering has to get on with things regardless of the metaphysics. Computers generate "random" numbers using deterministic algorithms called pseudo-random number generators, which produce sequences that pass statistical tests for randomness but are entirely reproducible if you know the starting seed — useful for simulations, dangerous if used for cryptography. For anything security-critical, systems instead harvest entropy from physical processes assumed to be genuinely unpredictable: thermal noise in circuits, timing jitter, or dedicated quantum random number generators that exploit photon behavior to produce numbers with a formal guarantee of unpredictability, not just a statistical one.

Why the Distinction Matters

The stakes are not purely philosophical. Cryptography depends on randomness that an adversary cannot predict even with unlimited computing power, which is only guaranteed if the source is ontologically random rather than merely complex. Evolutionary biology depends on mutation being effectively unpredictable at the level that matters for natural selection, whether or not it's "truly" random underneath. And our intuitions about free will are entangled with the question too: if a decision in the brain ultimately traces back to a quantum event, does that make the decision free, or just as uncaused and arbitrary as a die roll — arguably no more meaningfully "free" than pure determinism would be.

perspectives.title: Physics Perspective
perspectives.description: Standard quantum mechanics treats measurement outcomes as fundamentally undetermined, and Bell's theorem experimentally rules out large classes of hidden-variable explanations that would restore determinism.

perspectives.title: Philosophy of Science Perspective
perspectives.description: Deterministic interpretations like Bohmian mechanics and many-worlds reproduce every quantum prediction while denying true randomness exists, showing the question may be interpretive rather than empirically decidable.

perspectives.title: Computer Science Perspective
perspectives.description: Pseudo-random number generators are fully deterministic algorithms that merely look random statistically, which is why cryptography instead relies on physical entropy sources with a formal unpredictability guarantee.

perspectives.title: Mathematics Perspective
perspectives.description: Algorithmic information theory defines a sequence as 'random' if it cannot be produced by any shorter description than itself, reframing randomness as a property of compressibility rather than causation.

perspectives.title: Evolutionary Biology Perspective
perspectives.description: Mutation is treated as random with respect to fitness, meaning unpredictable relative to what an organism needs, which is a functional definition of randomness independent of any deeper physical fact.

openQuestions: If a future experiment definitively favored a deterministic interpretation of quantum mechanics, would anything in physics or daily life actually need to change?
Can a purely deterministic universe still contain events that are random in every sense that matters practically, or is the distinction only philosophical?
Does the existence (or non-existence) of true randomness have any bearing on whether human choices can be considered free?
Is there a way to experimentally distinguish 'true' quantum randomness from a deterministic process too complex for us to ever decode?
